hints: Start by recalling the chromosome number in each gamete compared to a normal body cell, and what happens to nuclei when they fuse.
Think about what the word diploid means in terms of sets of chromosomes, and where each set in the zygote has come from.
Now link the two sets together - why does one chromosome from the mother and one from the father count as a homologous pair with matching features?
walkthrough:
From Two Haploid Cells to One Cell**
Each gamete is haploid, so it carries only one set of chromosomes after meiosis. At fertilisation the two haploid nuclei fuse, so their chromosome sets add together in a single nucleus. That is the zygote.

Why This Is Diploid**
Diploid means having two complete sets of chromosomes. Because one full set came from the male gamete and one full set came from the female gamete, the new cell has $1n + 1n = 2n$. That restores the diploid number.

Why These Are Homologous Chromosomes**
For every chromosome contributed by the mother there is a matching chromosome contributed by the father. They are the same length, have the centromere in the same position and carry the same genes at the same loci. One maternal plus one paternal chromosome therefore makes a homologous pair.

Final answer: Fertilisation fuses two haploid gametes to form a diploid cell; the diploid cell contains two sets of chromosomes, one set from each gamete. One set is maternal and one is paternal, forming homologous pairs with the same genes, loci, size and centromere position.

hints: Focus on the difference between meiosis I and meiosis II - in which division does the chromosome number halve, and what is still joined at that point?
Recall what separates in anaphase I compared to anaphase II - whole chromosomes versus sister chromatids - and use that to justify the stage.
walkthrough:
Where Halving Happens**
Reduction division means the chromosome number is halved from diploid to haploid. That happens in meiosis I, seen at anaphase I moving into telophase I. Meiosis II is like mitosis and does not reduce chromosome number.

What Separates and Why It Reduces Number**
In anaphase I, whole homologous chromosomes of each bivalent are pulled to opposite poles. Sister chromatids stay together at this stage. Because the two members of each homologous pair go to different daughter cells, each daughter cell gets only one set of chromosomes, so the number is halved.
Final answer: anaphase I / telophase I; because homologous chromosomes / bivalents separate, halving the chromosome number.

hints: Look carefully at how many cells are present and where the dark-stained chromosomes lie - lined up in the middle or pulled to the ends?

Remember that after meiosis I the cell divides into two, so a picture showing two side-by-side plates belongs to meiosis II, while a single cell with chromosome groups at opposite poles belongs to meiosis I.
walkthrough:
Reading Fig. 4.1**
Fig. 4.1 shows the cell has already divided into two compartments with a wall between them. In each compartment the chromosomes are lined up across the equator of the spindle. Two metaphase plates in two haploid cells is the hallmark of metaphase II.

Reading Fig. 4.2**
Fig. 4.2 shows a single cell with two dark groups of chromosomes pulled right to opposite poles and a clear space in the middle. Whole chromosomes have separated and reached the poles but cytokinesis has not yet divided the cell. That matches late anaphase I to telophase I.
Final answer: Fig. 4.1: metaphase II (accept anaphase II); Fig. 4.2: telophase I (accept anaphase I).

hints: Work backwards from the end product - if each haploid product has 12 chromosomes, what is the diploid number, and how many chromatids does each replicated chromosome contain at the start of meiosis?
walkthrough:
From Haploid Product to Starting Chromatids**
Each cell at the end of meiosis has 12 chromosomes, so $n = 12$. The pollen mother cell is diploid, so $2n = 24$ chromosomes. DNA replication before meiosis makes each chromosome consist of two sister chromatids, so $24 \times 2 = 48$ sister chromatids at the start of meiosis.
